result.markdown: --- title: "03 · Multiple regression" subtitle: "Week 1" --- ::: {.guiding-q} What if there are several predictors? ::: ## In this session - Partial effects: the effect of one predictor *holding the others constant* - Why simple and multiple regression can give different answers - Standardising predictors (z-transformation) and comparing effects - Collinearity and variance inflation - Diagnostics in multiple regression ::: {.key-terms} **Key terms:** [Collinearity](../../glossary.qmd#collinearity), [z-transformation (standardisation)](../../glossary.qmd#z-transformation), [Centring](../../glossary.qmd#centring) ::: ## Learning goals After this session you can - fit and interpret a model with several predictors, - explain why an estimate changes when another predictor is added, - diagnose collinearity. ## Simulate first Age and body size are correlated, but only age affects the response. The simple regression on size finds an "effect" that disappears once age is in the model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(3) n <- 200 age <- rnorm(n) size <- 0.7 * age + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7) # size depends on age y <- 1 + 0.5 * age + rnorm(n) # y depends on age only round(coef(lm(y ~ size)), 2) # size seems to matter ... ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> (Intercept) size #> 0.99 0.35 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(coef(lm(y ~ size + age)), 2) # ... until age is controlled for ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> (Intercept) size age #> 1.00 0.01 0.50 ``` ::: ::: ## Materials ::: {.materials} - Slides coming soon - R script coming soon - Exercises coming soon ::: ## Reading - Gelman, Hill & Vehtari (2020), ch. 10–11. - Fox (2016), ch. 5 and 13.
